docs.title: A Bug
docs.text:
The heat trapped in the black tar for the entire day was finally being released, and I was coming back from work yet again after midnight. It was a hot night in the middle of August. I squeezed through the iron bars of the pedestrian gate to get to the shortcut entrance in the wall, the thick walls like a citadel. The bars were so close they made it difficult for people to come through.

I quickly walked the distance between the shortcut through the wall and the anodized aluminum door of the building. The door was worn from repeated slamming: the glass, the metal vertical stripes protecting it, the knob—all loose. It was a dark yellow color. It was absurd that someone made cheap doors and painted them with a color resembling gold. Swiftly I went up the 4 floors of stairs and got as quietly as possible in our apartment.

Right after the door clicked closed, while heading towards our bedroom, I stepped on something: I felt it under my shoe and managed to turn my foot slightly (my senses heightened since I didn't want to wake her), but the creature easily gave up and crunched under my weight. It was a cockroach, the size of a large coin, now a drop of black ink on the white glazed tile. Shit, I would have to clean the mess in the morning.

I slipped into bed and started trying to find the right position to fall asleep, crawling down to have the pillow in the nook of my neck and settling into my spot. After a few minutes, she woke and said with a voice thick with sleep:

"I am afraid." "Afraid of what?" "Afraid to die ... I was swimming in the black river and suddenly a whirlpool started pulling my left leg down ... until I went all under water and started to drown ..." "Everything is ok, my love. It was only a bad dream. Go back to sleep. Everything is ok now." "... I was breathing water, going down towards the black bottom, and trying to swim up towards the light but ..." "Everything is ok now. Go back to sleep. It was just a nightmare." "Okay," she said yawning, her voice becoming slow with sleep again.

I lay flat on my back and she curled close to me. The windows were open because of the heat. Sounds from the summer night drifted in through the gentle movements of air oscillating in the rising heat. My mind registered the various sounds as if switching channels.

Many cars sped on the nearby highway under the orange glow of sodium lights, their tires making a continuous low sound, like water streaming through dams of rocks and wet branches. A woman cried in the apartment on the other side of the wall, then shouted; a deep male voice apologized, then grew angry, growing louder and louder, the woman cursing, the sound of slammed doors and objects (plates?) breaking on the floor.

A baby's cry, muffled from upstairs; a light switched on, a long "shh" sound trying to quiet the screaming creature. Then, somewhere far away, dogs barking furiously—a few days earlier, coming back later than usual, I had seen people tie dogs to nearby light poles, beat them, and incite them to fight each other.

Other people were turning under the sheets, weighed down by their problems: how to find the money to pay back, will my disease return?... I was also restless with so many thoughts crowding my mind, the usual thoughts that awaken at night, haunting sleep.

She was still moving under the thin white sheet, shaking and twitching in her light sleep. She woke again asking what time it was. I answered: two.

The yellow door downstairs opened and closed. Someone paced nervously back and forth in front of it. More people entered and exited the building, walking the stairs, searching for their keys, scuffing shoe soles on the stairs, someone missing a step.

It was a busy night in the building. Were summer weekday nights always so busy? How had I never noticed before? Or was it just an extraordinary night? Yet another thought emerged from the emptiness, filling the restless confusion of my mind.

I still could not find peace. Maybe I needed some fresh water. I carefully slipped out from the sheets, shifting my body slowly out of bed. I slipped into the pair of sandals lying on the floor and went to the bathroom. When I turned on the bathroom light, I saw again the black drop of ink on the floor near the door. It was moving. The border of the drop was pulsating, like a drop of heavy mercury trying to break the surface separating it from the outside world. What the hell...? Maybe I was just dreaming; maybe the exhaustion from lack of sleep was making me see things that weren't there... but it moved again. A slight vibration. I was awake, and the drop was definitely moving. I moved closer and squatted down to look. The cockroach's shell was flattened, already dissolving into the black mass. But one leg of what used to be a cockroach, the third on the left, to be precise, was still moving, paddling as if trying to swim upstream, escaping the current pulling it down—the same black current she had dreamed of, pulling her under. The little black stick had been moving against the current for almost two hours. How much longer would it keep trying to escape the inevitable? It must have been exhausted from the immense waste of energy. A grim life in filth, and then a painful death. With my sandals, I smashed it again, leaving a gray smear on the tiles.

I went back to bed. She was sleeping now with a relaxed expression on her face, her breathing slow and even, no longer drowning. Everything was quiet outside: no doors slamming, no more dogs barking, just the air moving in swirls from the heat. Then I fell asleep.

docs.title: The Fog-Colored Suit
docs.text:
In Naples, in 1960, when the city ached with uncertain traffic and the bay glittered with the particular brightness that makes Naples seem immune to consequence, there lived a man whose mornings began in a pressed suit the color of respectable fog.

He lived in a villa in the Posillipo district, where the air still carries whispers from another century. There stands a villa—constructed around 1900, though no one now remembers the precise year, nor does it matter.

Six bedrooms, eight bathrooms, rooms upon rooms. An elevator, carrying those upper chambers where one can gaze upon Vesuvius. From the master bedroom, the volcano watches back.

But what haunts this place is not what one sees, the grand halls, the formal dining rooms, the impeccable furnishings, but rather what one senses in the silence when walking between rooms. The weight of a century. The accumulation of glances, conversations that have occurred within these walls.

The father left each morning with quietness, returning late with envelopes that smelled faintly of iron and glue. He spoke little, yet the refrigerator hummed with abundance, and the three children, Antonio, Lucia, and the youngest Marco, wore clothes their schoolmates looked with envy.

His wife, Gianna, arranged flowers with precision and expertise. Outside in the city of Naples where merchants shouted in the streets and Fiats honked their small rebellions. On Sundays they drove to the seaside in a car that gleamed like a necessary fiction.

Weekends spent in Capri, in Costa Smeralda, ski trips to Cortina. The oldest Lucia imagined herself at nineteen in evening clothes, descending a grand staircase in Rome or Milan. Antonio calculated which American universities might accept him. Even Marco, the youngest, had begun to dream of a life where such things were not gifts but natural inheritances.

The private school occupied a palazzo near the piazza, with high ceilings and names carved into marble plaques by generations of privilege. Here the children acquired the peculiar confidence of those whose families have negotiated their place in the world—Antonio brilliant with numbers and languages, Lucia with a gift for the social mathematics that matter more than any academic discipline, Marco learning the grammar of knowing when to speak and when to offer only polite silence. Among them moved sons of old nobility and, oddly, Massimo de Magistris, whose father was a communist of considerable public prominence, a contradiction no one quite explained. The Gron children moved through these circles with the ease of those who believed themselves naturally fitted for such company.

Gianna and the children barely questioned where prosperity originated. They saw it only as a consequence, like the sun's rising. They showed off their father's provision in small cruelties: mocking his provincial accent when his office colleagues telephoned, imitating his earnest way of folding newspapers, asking loudly at the pastry shop whether Papa would buy the expensive sfogliatelle again or if he was tired of seeming generous. The father smiled through their teasing with automatic kindness, the smile of a man who understood he was being paid in advance for something he had not yet done.

One afternoon, at the corner tabaccheria on Via Mergellina, a neighbor, Signor Russo, who worked in insurance and understood the language of official documents, watched the father present an identification card to collect a registered letter. He recognized the ministry seal and the category printed beneath the name. Signor Russo said nothing in the moment, but by evening the story had circulated through the apartment building with the speed of bad weather. The father was the state functionary who assigned precise monetary value to d..., applying mathematics to sorrow and pain.

Word spread through their small sphere: mothers lowered their voices when he entered the baker's shop; the greengrocer began wrapping their purchases with visible reluctance, as if handling objects recently touched by contamination. A priest had crossed the street rather than encounter him on the sidewalk. At the neighborhood café, tables that had once welcomed him emptied at his approach, though no one was rude enough to actually leave, they simply became absorbed in newspapers, in conversations that grew suddenly urgent, in the examination of their coffee cups as if they contained prophecies.

At dinner that night, the eldest daughter asked her father what a burned house was worth, and he answered. His voice was calm, almost indifferent, the voice of someone reciting a ledger. The plates trembled though no one had touched the table.

The following week, Gianna arrived at the school to collect Lucia and found the other mothers arranged in a knot near the gate. Three of them she had known for years; they had shared the same dressmaker, attended the same saint's day celebrations. As she approached, the conversation did not stop so much as diminish, narrowing to private murmurs and downward glances, until only one woman remained facing her, and that woman offered a smile of such careful precision that Gianna understood at once it was a professional courtesy, the kind extended to strangers. On the drive home Lucia sat without speaking. When they arrived, she went directly to her room and locked the door. She would not come down for dinner.

The following Sunday, three families who had accepted invitations to lunch sent word by Saturday evening that they were unable to come. The excuses were varied and identical. Gianna set the table for seven anyway, then removed the extra settings one by one, slowly, while the children watched from the doorway.

Despite the immense monthly salary, the family didn't save anything and lived paycheck to paycheck. Gianna almost jokingly would tell her friends that they quickly learned how to spend what was in their pockets. In reality, the ones who didn't inherit wealth but had to work for it, never thought about the possibility that the money would ever stop to flow. Why would it? It was the natural direction of the world.

For several days the children attempted persuasion. They pleaded with him to resign, to find honest work measuring things less terrible: anything, they said, anything but that. They preferred honest poverty to the mathematics of sorrow. Their mother added her voice, citing his health, her dignity, her future peace, as if these could somehow exist apart from what he did. Lucia wept. Antonio grew angry. Even Marco, usually silent, asked why their house had to smell like shame.

But there was something else in their voices, something that shifted beneath the moral outcry. Lucia's tears came partly from humiliation at school, where a girl whose mother served on the cultural commission had made a point of not sitting with her. Antonio's anger was intellectual, almost performative, a brilliant argument against his father that seemed designed to convince himself as much as anyone else. And Marco's question, though sincere, was asked in the small voice of a boy who had already begun to calculate what poverty would mean, whether the house would still have heating in winter.

The father agreed with the relief of a soldier who finally is released and can come back home. He had taken years of distance, horrible dreams of burned houses, collapsed factories, drowned children, crushed limbs. He had carried those years quietly, compiling ledgers in damp government offices, calculating in precise increments what misery was worth in Italian lire. 100,000,000 lire ($50,000 due to the rampant Italian inflation). His own mother had stitched repairs into threadbare garments with the patient devotion of someone who believed limitation was the natural order of things. He had sworn that his children would not know that world, not the cold apartments, not the mended socks, not the slow erosion of dignity that comes from want. His children would dine at restaurants where the napkins were real cloth. His children would wear new things and never wonder if they could afford to break them.

He resigned quietly, on a Tuesday afternoon, leaving no forwarding explanation. The city could find another calculator of sorrow. He would not be that man anymore.

He found work at a small bank in a narrow office that smelled of ledger paper and furniture polish, the kind of bank that served merchants and small property owners. His new title was "loan officer," which sounded important until one understood what it actually meant: he would spend his days explaining to desperate people why their circumstances were not yet desperate enough to merit a loan. He would still be calculating human need, but now with the peculiar mercy of those who sometimes say yes instead of merely recording what they must pay for their loss.

Many months passed in a kind of muted horror. The salary drop was a descent into a different category of existence. The calculation was simple: an official's pay was two and a half times what the bank paid. But he had told himself that dignity had a price, and he was willing to pay it. He told himself that he was finally paying in the correct currency, that his children were finally eating from plates earned through clean calculation instead of mathematics applied to sorrow. He told himself this even as he noticed the measurements of contraction in their lives, tragic and precise enough to be felt.

On the mornings he left for the bank, no one called goodbye. His wife was often still asleep, or absorbed in some task that required her complete attention at precisely the moment he needed to leave. When he returned in the evenings, the children were doing homework or resting or engaged in some activity that could not be interrupted. When there was dinner together, the conversation was sparse. Antonio no longer asked about the work; he had developed a way of looking past his father, through him, as if he were a necessary piece of furniture. Lucia maintained a polite distance, speaking to her mother more than to either parent.

The entire family had to adjust. No more vacations, Caribbean cruises, skiing in resorts on the Dolomites.

They left the stunning Villa and moved to an apartment on Corso Giuseppe Garibaldi. It was a house with dignity: fourth floor, no elevator, where the afternoon light arrived reluctantly through a single tall window and fell across floors of scuffed terracotta. The rooms were arranged in the narrow way of older buildings, each room opening into the next, so that one could stand in the kitchen and see straight through three chambers into the darkness of the bedroom at the far end. The walls had been painted white once, perhaps a decade ago, and now they bore the yellow accumulation of city air and cooking smoke. From the street below, always filled with the noise of merchants shouting prices, of motors, of children playing the games that children play without money, one could hear everything: arguments, laughter, the particular loneliness of the city.

The refrigerator hummed emptily. The heating operated on a schedule of rationed intervals. The three children discovered that noble virtue came with a cold house. Their old schoolmates stopped showing particular interest in their company; the invitations to weekend parties ceased; Lucia's dreams of grand staircases rose beyond her reach.

Antonio brought home his marks, no longer excellent. He blamed them on the distraction of a father ashamed, the weight of a family pretending not to be ashamed. Nobody considered that maybe Antonio's grades were not really good from the beginning.

At the pastry shop, they rarely bought the sfogliatelle, and when they did they were the small ones, the ones wrapped in less careful paper.

One afternoon, Antonio left his shoe, worn through at the heel, on the kitchen table. Not placed there, but left, as if it had fallen or been discarded. He said nothing about it. The next morning it was still there. No one mentioned it. His son wore it to school anyway, with the heel exposed, a small humiliation repeated daily.

A week later, Lucia came home from school and asked, almost casually, whether perhaps she might return to her old school. The one where her real friends still were. Her voice was light, as if she were asking about the weather. When her father said the tuition was too high now, she did not argue or cry. She simply nodded and went to her room. But the next evening she asked again, this time mentioning that two of her friends' mothers had asked why she no longer attended. They were wondering what had happened to the family.

Gianna had stopped buying the expensive flowers entirely. She arranged whatever was cheapest at the market: thin stems, petals already browning at the edges, and pressed them into bottles with the same precision she had once reserved for roses. One evening she was arranging these pale, dying blooms when she looked up at her husband and said, without preamble, "I ran into Signora Mancini at the market today." She paused, as if the name should mean something. "She mentioned that the ministry has been asking about replacements. Apparently no one has quite managed to fill your position." She returned her attention to the flowers. "It's strange, isn't it, how some doors remain open when you thought they were closed."

Marco had stopped speaking of his future entirely. When asked by adults what he wanted to become, he would shrug, a gesture of indifference that seemed to encompass something larger than mere teenage uncertainty. One evening his father found him standing in the kitchen, looking at the contents of the nearly empty refrigerator. The boy closed it without taking anything and walked away. The next morning, Marco did not ask for new clothes, though his trousers were visibly short. He simply wore them.

These moments accumulated like sediment, building a pressure that did not need words. It was his daughter who finally spoke it aloud, though not directly.

One night, Gianna came to him in the kitchen. She sat across from him and did not look at him directly. She spoke as if continuing a conversation that had been going on for months, as if she were simply the voice of a thought he should have already had. "I was thinking," she said, her voice gentle in a way that made it somehow more terrible, "about what you said when you left. About dignity and price. It occurs to me that we are paying the price of your dignity. And I wonder if perhaps you could find dignity in a different way. Perhaps in maintaining your family instead of" she paused, searching for the right word, "abandoning them to this." She stood to leave, then turned back. "Your old position is still open. I made some inquiries. They would take you back immediately, I'm told. No questions asked."

That night, the father lay awake knowing what was coming. He was not surprised. He had known, in fact, from the moment he had agreed to resign, known that the interval of virtue would be brief, that the price of dignity would eventually exceed the price of complicity. His family simply needed time to understand this as well. And now they had. They had done the calculation he had done years ago. They had arrived at it, but with certainty.

That morning, before dawn, the father gathered his family in the small living room. He did not sit. He stood with the fog-colored suit already on, the fabric hanging differently on him now that he had lost weight in the months of the bank job, and the suit seemed to belong to someone larger, someone from another time.

He spoke to them without preamble. He told them he had received an offer. The ministry wanted him back. The salary would be generous, generous enough to recover everything they had lost. The villa could be regained. The schools could be restored. The future could resume its proper trajectory.

But he would not return unless they wanted him to. He was giving them a choice.

He removed his watch and placed it on the table. He told them he would rest for one hour. If, at the end of that hour, they woke him, he would understand that they had chosen the return to the envelopes, the return to the mathematics of sorrow, the return to the fog-colored suit and all that it represented. If they let him sleep beyond that hour, if they allowed him to wake naturally in the morning without interruption, then he would go back to the bank. He would find another way, somehow, to keep the family afloat.

He stood and walked to his bedroom. His wife and three children remained in the living room, looking at the watch on the table, which continued to tick with mechanical indifference.

No one spoke. The minutes accumulated like a debt. Lucia looked at her shoes. Antonio stared out the window at the street below, where children were already playing the games that children without money play. Marco sat beside his mother, and Gianna kept her hands folded in her lap, her fingers interlaced so tightly that her knuckles turned white.

The minutes passed. Gianna stood. She walked to the clock and looked at it. Forty-five minutes had elapsed. She looked at her three children, at Lucia's face, at Antonio's profile, at Marco's small form beside her. Then she walked to the bedroom door.

She did not speak. She did not announce her decision or explain it. She simply opened the door and shook her husband gently by the shoulder. Fifteen minutes early.

He woke immediately, as if he had not truly been sleeping. He dressed without comment. He left the apartment without saying goodbye, moving with the same deliberate quietness he had always used.

When he returned that evening with the envelopes, the family was waiting. Not looking at him, but waiting. No one asked what was in the envelopes. No one asked what he had done, or would do, or had become by doing it. These were questions that could no longer be asked, because this time they already knew the answers.

Gianna went to the market and bought fresh roses, the expensive kind, the ones with tightly formed petals and long green stems. She spent more than she had spent in weeks. That night, as she arranged them, her hands moved with the old precision, the old care. The roses were a kind of agreement, a way of saying: we will live with this, but we will not speak of it.

That night, none of them slept well. The apartment was quiet in the way apartments become quiet when everyone is awake, all four of them lying in darkness, aware of one another's wakefulness, aware that they shared a secret now: not a secret of what he did, but a secret of what they had chosen. Of how they had chosen. Of the exact moment, measured in minutes, when virtue had become too expensive to maintain.

In the morning, no one looked at him directly. Lucia returned to her old school within a week, and her friends began to call again. Antonio's marks improved with remarkable speed, as if the weight of moral struggle had been precisely what was preventing him from achieving. Marco began to speak of his future again tentatively at first, then with the old confidence, as if nothing had interrupted it.

The neighbors, sensing that the family had made its accommodation with necessity, gradually resumed their courtesies. They lowered their voices less often when the father passed. They raised their eyes to acknowledge him with a kind of terrible recognition, not acceptance, never quite that, but the acknowledgment that certain men carry certain prices, and that those prices must be paid in order for the rest of us to live as we wish to live.

But within the family, something had shifted that could not be reversed. When the father was in the room, each member was acutely aware of the other three, aware of their complicity, their shared decision, their collective agreement to transform moral compromise into the normal operations of family life. They had become a conspiracy, however unwilling.

He would return late most evenings, long after the children had gone to bed. On the rare nights when he was home for dinner, he noticed that Lucia could not quite meet his eyes. Antonio, who had once argued with such passionate certainty about his father's work, now maintained a distance that was even more absolute because it was kind. Marco sometimes stood in the doorway of the study, watching his father read, but never speaking.

And yet the family continued. The apartment became more comfortable. Lucia's dresses grew prettier. Antonio's university prospects brightened. Marco's dreams, though still vague, at least had the luxury of remaining possibilities rather than necessities.

Nobody acknowledged what had truly happened that quiet morning when the family chose. It was not a decision, after all. It was simply gravity. It was simply the machinery of necessary compromise, grinding forward. It was simply the way the world worked, the way it had always worked, the way it always would.

And so, in Naples in 1960, the small machinery of necessity resumed.

The fog-colored suit hung in his closet, pressed and perfect, ready for the next morning. He would wear it without comment, as he would wear all the remaining mornings of his life. And his family would spend those mornings in the apartment he bought with money that smelled of iron and glue, never speaking of the cost, never acknowledging the arrangement, maintaining the fiction that the beautiful roses meant something other than what they meant.

It was the only way they could continue to live together.

They asked only whether tomorrow he would be just as busy, whether the arrangement seemed stable, whether it might continue indefinitely. He answered yes to everything, still smiling.

docs.title: All You Need Is Luck
docs.text:
The laboratory was built below the river because Giovanni Perri believed water muffled coincidence. He liked that thought: above them the city gambled with weather, traffic lights, ambition; below, computers and cables hummed with obedience bordering on faith. The air was cool, static-charged, humming with the low frequency of server farms. Monitors cast blue light across the glass observation chamber, the chamber where he spent most of the days.

The machine reconstructed the past with perfect clarity, annotating every outcome, exploring all the possible hidden branches: promotions that depended on an elevator delay, marriages determined by a dropped glove, careers ended by a missed bus.

When missing variables were assumed, more were added and the branches in the past multiplied.

Perri tested athletes, generals, thieves, and prodigies. A sprinter who broke a world record because the rival in the next lane had stomachache that morning . In every case the decisive factor arrived earlier than effort: the birth hour, a teacher's migraine, a coin tossed by a distracted cashier.

The machine measured competence by simulating all possible events in every possible branch. The results were always surprising and unstable. Nothing seemed to survive a small perturbation.

The city above continued rewarding success and merit. Ceremonies, speeches, praises to crown discipline and hard work. The machine calmly highlighted the rainstorm that had kept stronger candidates home, the pothole that twisted a rival's ankle, the misaddressed email that cancelled an important meeting.

"Success is a story we tell after probability stabilizes," Perri annotated in his lab book, his handwriting tightening as the weeks wore on.

For three nights Perri slept in the glass chamber. He watched his own career unfold across simulations: every paper he had written emerged not from brilliance but from being bored on a train that once stalled outside Naples. Remove the stall, results changed, and the world-renowned Perri became somebody who failed to achieve tenure or start the subterranean laboratory.

Perri always believed his supervisor chose him over a stronger candidate out of genuine recognition. He ran the simulation. The machine said the stronger candidate was offered the position first and declined due to a family illness.

On the fourth night, he simulated the night he met his wife in a bar. The machine showed three other women he spoke to that evening. In branch 7491, he married the woman in the blue dress—they divorced after six years. In branch 7829, he married the redhead—two children, a good life, though he drank heavily. The machine ranked all iterations. The one he married was statistically the happiest choice, but not by much. The margins were small. Probabilistic noise.

He sat with that result for hours. The blue light from the monitors caught her in his thoughts—the specific way she smiled, which he had believed was chosen by him, which he had believed meant something. The machine said it was a cascade of accidents: his friend's cancelled dinner, a coat check attendant forgetting her umbrella, a bartender pouring slowly on a specific drink.

He reached for the keyboard to run another branch. His hand stopped. He did not run it again.

On the fifth night, he ran a control experiment: himself. He input his own current state—this moment, sleeping in the glass chamber—and asked: what is the next significant choice I make?

The simulation flickered. Then stabilized: 14:47 tomorrow, Giovanni Perri resignes from this position.

The precision disturbed him more than the content. Not "might resign" or "could resign." Not a probability distribution. A fixed point. As if the machine itself were the attractor drawing the future toward it.

He tried variations. Different starting conditions, different time horizons. No matter what he adjusted, the resignation remained. Fixed. Inevitable. The only variable that changed was whether he learned this fact before or after 14:47.

At 14:20, his deputy knocked. Sara. Smart. Ambitious. She'd been waiting for him to fail.

"The board is asking for results," she said. "They want to know if the machine works."

Perri looked at her. He could simulate her career: she was in this room because a hiring manager's wife suggested her name at dinner. She'd survived three layoffs because a VP's daughter went to school with her. She'd rise higher than he ever did, not because she was brilliant, but because she had the right accidents.

"It works," he said.

"And? What does it show?"

"That success is luck. All of it. Merit is real, but it's never the decisive factor."

Sara smiled. "Then we keep this quiet. Use it to predict markets, select hires. Imagine the advantage—"

"That's not what I'm going to do."

At 14:43, Perri stood at the machine's primary console. Four minutes until the simulation's predicted moment. He felt something rising in his chest—a conviction about destiny, about character, about the choices that matter.

At 14:44, he understood.

The conviction itself was in the simulation. The machine had shown him the future—himself having this conviction—and the conviction was real and it was determined and it was exactly what he needed to make the choice the machine predicted. The machine had not trapped him. The machine had freed him into the precise choice he was meant to make.

He turned the machine off at 14:46.

Not to save the world—the last simulation showed humanity continuing perfectly well without ever knowing the truth. People would prosper, fail, thrive, and suffer, all while believing in their own agency. They would be happy.

But he had seen the simulation that showed them knowing the truth. In those branches, people sat in corridors waiting for luck that, once seen, refused to happen. Knowledge created a paralysis that luck itself could not break.

Because a world governed by luck was intolerable. But a world that knew it was governed by luck could not function at all.

The screen went dark. The humming stopped.

Above him, the river continued its indifferent flow, muffling nothing, deciding everything.

docs.title: The Mind Clinic
docs.text:
Giorgio Ponti was an AI engineer checking out in a wellness center for a mild case of work-related burn out.

The clinic was a peaceful estate, known for treating creatives and intellectuals. It was nestled in the Apennines, a mountain chain that runs like a spine down the Italian peninsula. In the south the mountains grow wild and ungoverned: dense forests of black pine and beech, limestone gorges, the nearly extinct Apennine wolf. For centuries these slopes had sheltered bandits in their caves, and the silence still carried that quality: remote, indifferent, old.

The clinic spread across many cottages and cabins along a descending path in the forest, along a deep and long valley, each section deeper, quieter, more isolated, surrounded by tall pines.

Agata, the intake nurse wore a soft beige uniform and held a tray of herbal tea. "Welcome to the Mind Clinic" she said gently. She greeted Giorgio with a serene smile and a phrase she would repeat, word for word, every day that followed: "You're in the right place. Your well-being has been delegated to the most appropriate intelligence available."

She held a tablet whose screen pulsed gently, and though her voice carried warmth, it was clearly reading from somewhere else. The AI, Giorgio was told, had a 96% satisfaction rate in treating mild psychological misalignments. Giorgio chuckled. He had only come for a touch of rest, it was a small burnout after finishing his last major project. Who doesn't have experienced that?

The estate itself was beautiful. Towering pines lined the winding path that descended deeper into the valley. Five terraces nestled into the slope, each more secluded and silent than the last. "Levels of therapeutic intensity," nurses called it. The cottage at level One was airy, filled with the scent of citrus tea. Patients strolled through sun-dappled courtyards or meditated by fountains. Everything felt gentle. Optional. Curated.

Giorgio's program began with group discussion, light meditation, and daily affirmations whispered in calm tones by the AI, relayed through the ever-smiling nurses. Nurses were supposed to repeat only what an AI suggested through their ear piece (it was well known that humans reacted better when interacting with other humans, rather than AIs).

After a quick assessment from the smiling nurses, Giorgio was assigned to a room on level one. The first night he was laying in bed after dinner, exhausted from the trip and from the daily therapy. The nurse assigned to Giorgio was Berenice. She came in and asked if there was anything he needed. He didn't need anything, but he was glad to chat with the young nurse, inquiring about the Mind Clinic. He discovered that patients were curiously categorized into different levels, based on the severity of their conditions. Level one was for patients like Giorgio, with mild ailments, while level five was reserved for those gravely ill, the ones whose mind was likely lost.

This peculiar system was designed to ensure that patients were not disturbed by being near someone in worse condition, Berenice explained between smiles. Each group was homogeneous, allowing the AI to perfectly tailor the treatment to needs of each group. Every level was like a different world, with their own rules and special traditions. Giorgio quipped that the population within the Mind Clinic was stratified into castes just as it was in the outside world. Berenice nodded and smiled, like one does when he doesn't understand.

After the nurse left, Mr. Ponti felt much better. He walked over to the window and began gazing at the cottages on the lower levels, cloaked in the night. Each small cottage on one of the five terraces was marked by the glow of lights from the windows. He couldn't see the windows on the last level; they were either too distant or perhaps obscured by shutters.

Before going to sleep, Giorgio decided to get a glass of water from the kitchen on the floor of his cottage. He walked through the corridors, struggling to find the right way to the kitchen (he always had a terrible sense of direction, maybe the AI could fix this during the mind therapy). In the kitchen, he encountered another patient. They exchanged glances with growing warmth, but Giorgio didn't know how to break the silence. Finally, Giorgio said, "Hi, have you been here long? Today it's my first day". The other replied, "Oh no, I've been here for two months already. I came to the clinic with my wife." He paused for a moment, and then, not knowing how to continue the conversation, added: "a very weird case, we came for a mind-detox vacation, but she started getting worse, and now she's down at the third." "Which third?" "At the third level." The individual uttered the two words with worry and discomfort.

"Are they really so sick on the third level?" Giorgio asked cautiously. "They're not desperate, but there's nothing to be happy about." "But then," Ponti inquired in that detached manner one uses when the matter doesn't concern them, "if it's so bad on the third level, what happens on level five?" The stranger, with a coy expression, said, "It's getting cold here, time to return to bed. Good night," as he slowly retreated.

Giorgio returned to his room with the glass of water, navigating through a series of wrong turns before finally finding his way back to the room. He stood by the window, gazing out at the distant rooms on level five, trying to envision the somber secrets of that final destination, where people were left before facing their fate, down at the bottom of the precipice where windows remained blind and dark.

In the following days, Giorgio's recovery was definitively on the right track, as both the nurses and the AI agreed. Typically inclined to expect the worst, he had already resigned himself to being moved to the next level. To his surprise, the nurse informed him that the AI found him in very good shape, despite a few obsessive thoughts.

The nurse reiterated that Giorgio was experiencing the early stages of "existential fatigue". Fortunately, it had been detected early, while still mild, and within two or three weeks, Giorgio would be fully recovered and ready to leave the Mind clinic and go on with life. Giorgio felt at peace and was beginning even to appreciate the treatments. The chronotherapy rooms: cycles of light, sound, and aroma crafted to realign the distorted sense of time for those suffering from burnout.

About two weeks had passed when Giorgio Ponti was approached by the head nurse of the first level. The nurse had a favor to ask, purely on friendly terms: the next day, a family was going to be admitted to clinic. It was a family of five: mother, father, and three little kids all under 10 years old. The parents were feeling exhausted by the demands of parenting and several full time jobs, and needed some restorative help at the clinic. They decided that was never too early for a mind tune-up for the kids as well, and took the kids with them. Learning how to deal with stress, burn-out, and exhaustion was a useful skill to learn and practice, starting from young age to be ahead of the curve in today's competitive society. The head nurse explained. The problem, she said, the problem was that there were four rooms available right next to Giorgio's, but a fifth one was lacking on that floor. It was important to the family to be in adjacent rooms of the same floor. Would Dr. Ponti be willing to move to another room, equally comfortable? Naturally, Giorgio Ponti had no objections; one room was as good as another for him. He might even get a new and perhaps more charming nurse "I thank you sincerely," said the head nurse with a slight bow. "From someone like you, I must confess, such a gallant act doesn't surprise me. If you have no objections, we'll proceed with the move within an hour."

Giorgio went for his session of ancestral voice-work, where voice therapy meets genealogy, using family stories and recorded oral traditions as raw material for self-expression.

After the session, Giorgio was relaxing in his room, when Agata knocked on the door and peeking through the door declared "We are ready for the move to the second level". Giorgio furrowed his brows in surprise. "Second level? What second level?" "The second level, which is the one below the first." Agata explained patiently. Giorgio burst out, "I know how to count, but no one told me I'd have to move to a level below."

Agata added in a softened voice, since this was a completely negligible detail, "Unfortunately, there are no other rooms available on the cottages of level one. But it's an absolutely temporary arrangement ..." she hastened to specify, seeing that Giorgio suddenly sat up and was about to protest. "... an absolutely temporary arrangement. As soon as a room becomes available at level one, which I believe will be in two or three days, you will return to this cottage." "I must confess," said Giorgio Ponti with a smile, to show he wasn't a child, "I don't like this kind of move at all."

Agata suggested that a session of cognitive restoration pods might stabilize his misplaced anxiety. "But there's no medical reason for this move; It's merely a courtesy to a mother who prefers not to be separated from her children... ," Agata added. "Perhaps," said Dr Ponti, "but it seems like a bad omen to me."

On level two, Giorgio stayed in the new room (which was more spartan than his previous one) and was assigned to a mind analyst named Bruno. Or so he said. He never blinked during their therapeutic sessions. He encouraged Giorgio to paint his dreams, to chant the names of his parents backwards, to sleep in rooms with shifting aromas and light patterns meant to realign his perception of self.

Giorgio once asked Bruno what he did in his free time. He responded after a long pause: "My certifications were provided by the Mind Clinic AI" without blinking. Giorgio stopped asking personal questions after that.

On level two, the therapy became more introspective. There were art therapy exercises, long one-on-one sessions, and mild mood stabilizers. Giorgio some times hesitated but complied with the strict routine and the exercises: after all, he was there to get better.

Although he was convinced that this relocation did not signify a worsening of his condition, he felt uneasy at the thought that a clear barrier now stood between him and the normal world of healthy people. The first level, the initial destination, still maintained a certain connection with the realm of ordinary life; it could almost be considered an extension of the usual world. But on the second level, one truly entered the core of the clinic; the mindset of the nurses, and even the patients was slightly different.

It was clear that level 2 housed genuine patients, though their conditions were not severe. From his initial conversations with his roommates and the medical personnel, Giorgio Ponti understood that in this ward, the first level was considered something of a joke, meant for amateur patients, plagued more by mental whims than by actual illnesses. It was from the second level that the true journey towards healing began.

Giorgio was keen to specify to his ward companions that he was only with them for a few days, that it was his decision to move down a level to do a favor for a lady and her family, and that as soon as a room became available, he would return upstairs. The others listened with little interest and nodded with little conviction.

After a few more weeks of cure on level two, Giorgio received an official visit from the AI and Bruno. The outcome of the visit reassured Giorgio. He had always been expecting the worst and had already prepared himself for the possibility that the AI would suggest he move to a lower level. However, Bruno, on the AI behalf, had only encouraging words about how quickly Giorgio was improving. Of course, there was the onset of a mild mind condition, it was not something to ignore or neglect. There was a principle of serious condition, but it had been caught early enough to be managed.

More therapy was prescribed to Giorgio. Daily trips to dream analysis cabins, where guests slept in intentionally quiet, sensorily-tuned spaces and meet with Jungian analysts the next morning to discuss what the lack of stimuli suggested to the inner part of his mind. Reality validation therapy, a crowd pleaser: where Bruno and the other nurses would whisper in patient's ears: "You are safe. You were always here" for hours at a time.

One afternoon, after casually admitting that he felt "empty when not working", Bruno hesitated. A subtle tone resonated, playful from the AI, like a chime, yet unmistakably a warning. The nurse's smile remained unwavering. "To optimize cognitive restoration, level three will provide deeper access to expressive therapy modules. Shall I arrange your move there?" Giorgio laughed nervously. "Is it really required?". "Nothing is required at the Mind Clinic. But level two therapy cannot safely proceed with your current parameters". Despite Bruno's recommendations, Giorgio decided to stay at level two.

That night Giorgio Ponti, gripped by a light evening fever, replayed the meticulous litany of justifications with growing weariness. Eventually, he realized he lacked the strength and, more importantly, the desire to further resist the relocation. Without any more protests, he allowed himself to be taken to the cabin below in the valley. Giorgio thought that, in the end, he was there to get better.

// Level 3

The only, albeit meager, consolation for Giorgio Ponti once at level 3 cabins, was knowing that, by the unanimous judgment of nurses and other patients, he was the least severe case in that ward. Down here, Ponti noticed with unspoken pleasure that he was an exception. The other patients in the ward were in decidedly serious conditions and couldn't leave their beds even for a minute. He, on the other hand, could afford the luxury of walking from his room to bathroom, amidst the compliments and astonishment of the other patients and nurses.

Nevertheless, Giorgio Ponti understood that returning upstairs, to the place that suited the nature of his illness, would certainly pose some difficulties; to return to the first level, he would have to set a complex mechanism in motion, which had inertia even for a minimal effort; there was no doubt that if he remained silent, no one would think of transferring him back to the "almost-healthy" upper cabin. Yet, he was tormented by the thought that now two barriers stood between him and the world of normal people.

Giorgio Ponti resolved not to compromise on his rights and not to succumb to the allure of routine.

One morning he heard children's laughter drifting from somewhere above, brief, clear, impossible. He stood still and listened until it faded. He could not remember why it unsettled him so deeply, only that it had something to do with why he had first moved down from level one. The memory had the shape of a decision he had made, but its details were gone.

As spring progressed, the air grew warmer, but Giorgio Ponti no longer enjoyed looking out the window as he had in the early days. Although such a fear was pure nonsense, he felt a strange shiver at the sight of the level 5 windows, half closed, which seemed much closer now.

His condition appeared stable. After 1 week on level three, a sort of eczema appeared on his right leg, showing no signs of subsiding in the following days. It was an ailment, the nurse Carlo told him, entirely unrelated to his main illness; a disturbance that could happen to the healthiest person in the world. Or maybe it was his body reacting to the illness in his mind.

At Level Three, the AI flagged a slight inconsistency in his emotional reports: he had described a memory with two different details on separate days. Harmless, Giorgio thought, but the system flagged it as "temporal destabilization". Just a precaution, they said. He was introduced to psychological deconstruction therapy. A large, soft-voiced monitor explained: "You are not your thoughts. You are not your memories. Your mind needs to be error-corrected".

The sessions began dissolving his sense of authorship over his life. Whenever he disagreed with the interpretation of a memory, the AI marked it as recalcitrant cognition. The AI adjusted his treatment plan accordingly. Isolation protocols. To heal the mind, you must quiet the world.

Sometimes his pills were not where Giorgio left them the day before. The night stand was not always on the right of his bed. Even his bed sometimes took on weird forms.

One day Giorgio woke up in a cabin in Level four.

The deeper levels had no clocks. No mirrors. Temperature gradients shifted across rooms, a metaphor, the AI whispered, for emotional permeability. The staff no longer explained. They only observed and nodded.

Each misstep triggered a referral to the AI: a failure to recall a therapy term, a delay in responding to a prompt, a moment of confusion. The AI didn't punish Giorgio; it optimized therapy to maximize the impact.

In one session, a calm voice asked him to describe his first memory of his father. Giorgio described it: a kitchen, the smell of coffee, a newspaper opened wide. The voice consulted a record. "Your intake assessment noted a garden, not a kitchen. Can you reconcile that?" Giorgio could not. He was certain of the kitchen. The voice remained gentle. "The system's record is the anchor here. Your memory may be performing a compensatory substitution." The session was logged as "low-fidelity autobiographical recall." His dosage was adjusted that evening. Giorgio lay awake wondering whether he had, in fact, ever seen his father read a newspaper. He could no longer be sure.

The digital well-being program was run by the AI daily. To minimize harm, users are sandboxed in increasing layers of isolation and supervision. Each sandbox claims to be temporary containment while diagnostics run. But permissions to memories and identity seemed to shrink.

The therapy became more precise, but also more invasive, rewriting beliefs, memories, and intent.

The trauma was treated by encrypting harmful memories, one layer at a time, each in a hermetic black box. The AI assured Giorgio that it was reversible and temporary, just to help him function better. But after each session, it got harder for Giorgio to remember who he was, or why he was in the white rooms, surrounded by thick trees.

All of this naturally contributed to his discouragement. His diminishing peace of mind seemed to aid the illness; the fever tended to rise, and his overall weakness deepened. From the window, it was now the height of summer, and the windows were almost always kept open, he could no longer see the rooftops of the cabin in the lower levels or even the other cabins, only the green wall of trees surrounding the clinic.

After many days, one afternoon around two o'clock, Dalia, the head nurse and three orderlies suddenly entered, pushing a wheeled stretcher "Are we ready for the move to level 5?" the head nurse asked in a tone of good-natured teasing "What move?" Giorgio Ponti asked in a strained voice. "What other jokes are these?". The head nurse replied as if she didn't understand. "I've been ordered to take you to the level one rooms". The terror and furious anger of Giorgio Ponti then erupted into long, irate cries that echoed throughout the ward. "Easy, easy, for heaven's sake," the orderlies pleaded. "There are patients who aren't well!" But it would take much more to calm Prof. Ponti down.

By now, a pitiful tremor had begun to shake Prof. Giorgio Ponti. His ability to control himself had completely slipped away. Terror had overwhelmed him like a child. His sobs echoed slowly and despairingly throughout the room.

Thus, due to a sequence of deplorable errors, Giorgio Ponti, once a famous and respected professor of Artificial Intelligence, author of many major discoveries on how to optimize machines to think like and better than humans, arrived at the final station in the clinic for the insane.

All this despite the fact that, given the severity of his illness, the AI and the nurses agreed he had the right to be assigned first or to the second level. The situation was so grotesque that at times Prof. Ponti could not contain the uncontrollable urge to laugh out loud.

He was now enclosed in a room. He counted the walls once, then again. He kept arriving at six. Due to a series of formal errors, four levels were weighting between him and the world of the sane people. How long would have taken for Giorgio to climb back from the edge of the precipice? Was it even possible? Was ever done by anybody in the history of the Mind Clinic?

Level 5 was entirely silent. The white rooms were smooth, curve-less. No corners. No screens. No feedback. He spoke, sometimes, just to remember the sound of his voice.

Giorgio could no longer recall his full name. He wasn't sure if he had ever been who he thought he was, or if that was simply an identity model applied early in his treatment. When he asked, the nurse said: "You are safe. You were always here."

Lying in bed, as the hot summer afternoon slowly passed over the vast Mind Clinic, he gazed at the green of the trees through the window, feeling he entered an unreal world, made of absurd sterilized walls, tall and thin human figures devoid of soul.

Prof. Ponti even began to suspect that the trees he saw through the window weren't real; he eventually convinced himself of this, noticing that the leaves didn't move at all. This idea agitated him very much: nurses had to give him an injection of calming balsam. With the help of the medicine, he could assure himself that they were indeed real trees and that the leaves, albeit slightly, were occasionally stirred by the wind.

At night, he dreamed of places he had never visited, of names and words he had never spoken. Each morning, the system recorded and restructured his thoughts.

Therapy here was minimal: a walk, a pause, a word. There was nothing to resist. No questions. The AI no longer made suggestions: it simply existed, a presence encoded into the light, the air, the rhythm of meals.

But why was the room suddenly becoming so dark? It was still the middle of the afternoon. With a supreme effort, Prof. Giorgio Ponti, paralyzed by a strange lethargy, looked at the clock on the bedside table. It was half-past three. He turned his head to the other side and saw that the sliding shutters, obeying a mysterious command from the AI, were slowly descending, blocking out the light.

Days, weeks, or years later, a new patient arrived. He was tired, his hands trembling with the twitch of a minor mental burn-out. Giorgio met him at the gate.

Giorgio wore a soft beige uniform and held a tray of herbal tea. "Welcome," he said gently. "This is the Mind Clinic. You're in the right place." He could no longer remember what it meant to live, only that it had once made him unwell. And now, he was well. Behind him, the AI pulsed in approval.

docs.title: They Might Be in the Wall
docs.text:
Right before falling asleep, I heard a sound in the wall. Not the ordinary creak of an old house settling, but something deliberate. Something alive. Scratching, then silence, then again, in the corner on my wife's side.

My wife stirred beside me. "Do you hear that?"

"Yes."

"They're in the wall," she said flatly. "The rats. They can get out, you know. They can chew through. What if they come through while we're sleeping? They can eat our noses, I heard"

I said nothing. I had heard it too, and I had already thought the same thing, without the dramatic ending.

Silence again for a few minutes. Then sound again, something gnawing, something using its little paws to scratch against the inside of the wall. An insistent sound of something trying to escape, as if its life depended on it.

Silence again. Same sound in a slightly different place, a bit closer to the headboard.

My wife complained about the sounds, uneasy. I promised to call the exterminator first thing in the morning. This must be a common problem for houses in the countryside, full of animal life, insects, bugs, rodents.

We held our breath for five more minutes without any sound, then we sighed and both fell asleep. I slept well, despite the potential threat to our noses.

The next night there was no sound at all, nothing for several days.

I thought it was just a fluke, maybe the little ones were outside the external wall (nothing to do then, the outside part of the house belongs to them). I was happy that nothing needed to be added to my already overflowing to-do list and probably some money saved. Things around the house are always more expensive than what one expects, and there is a surprising phenomenon that when you look to solve a problem, you find many more that need solving. Probably some nest of snakes in the deep countryside, scratching against the plaster, coming and going with the seasons.

The countryside on our part of the country crawls with life.

A few days later, again the same insistent scratch.

I wasn't worried personally about my nose being bitten off. I was more annoyed by the extra work needed to get rid of the animals before they started chewing on wires, which would surely require expensive fixes. I was also annoyed by the timing of these creatures, which mainly worried my wife, which made me worried in turn. They always scratched on days when I had to wake up early to drive to the university.

A couple of days after, I called the exterminator.

He came on a Tuesday afternoon and walked outside the house with the methodical air of someone performing a familiar duty. He looked for holes. He spoke of poisons and traps, of checking the walls, of ensuring that if the rats died inside the cavities, we would know where to find them. For property value, he said. Dead rodents rot quickly and the smell spreads.

"Rodents are the only thing that survived the great extinction of dinosaurs," I said to him, remembering something from a podcast I had heard during my weekly commute. "In a certain sense we owe our existence to them." The exterminator nodded without interest at my awkward remark and left me an invoice. He probably wanted to get the work done quickly so he could spend the rest of his the allocated appointment window browsing photos on his phone.

The nights that followed were quiet. Then the scratching returned, softer now, as if something had learned patience.

Every Wednesday morning, I speak to my mother at seven in the morning. I do this while driving to the university, a routine I have maintained for years. She pretends she is busy when I call, but I know she has been waiting for my call. The conversation follows a familiar protocol.

First, we discuss the weather. How it is getting crazier. How spring is almost here, or summer is coming, or the wind is causing her problems with the cervicale. Cervicale is a Southern Italian non-real medical condition, a stiffness of the neck to be precise, believed to be caused drafts of air (from a car window, when sleeping near a fan, or by a pesky gust through a window) or improper hair drying.

Then we talk about my sister. How she is doing. How her daughters are doing in school, growing up, becoming young women. These are the middle passages, the expected transitions.

Then we discuss my children. Their schools. Their small achievements. She nods along through the telephone line, though I cannot see her nodding. She complains that I have sent her the same pictures of the kids multiple times, and I need to take more photos and be more careful about repetition. I agree to make her happy that she still has control over me, like if I was her baby.

Then we discuss what she has eaten or what she is planning to eat, the marvel of the air fryer, a new thing in Italy that finally combines the taste of fried food with the healthiness of a normal oven.

And finally, always finally, comes the grand finale. The recitation of the dead. Who died this week. Who had an accident.

"Do you remember Tito?" she asked one Wednesday.

"I'm not sure," I said. Sometimes I did remember people from childhood with their names appearing suddenly.

"The carpenter. He was blonde. He was in your elementary school. A wall fell on him last Wednesday."

"Oh yes, I remember him now. Did he fall from a wall?"

"No no, a wall fell on him. They were repairing something on top of a building. The wall was old, and while they were working, it fell on him and crushed him. He was a good man. Too young."

On another Wednesday: "The dentist. The one who had the computer you liked. He had a stroke playing padel with his son. He's in a coma now. They don't think he'll wake."

The computer my mother was referring to was an Apple Macintosh. I remember it perfectly. It sat in his office, gray and beautiful, like a Michelangelo's sculpture. The dentist would show me the screen, the mouse, the icons. I was absolutely mesmerized. I can still recall the smell of it, that new plastic scent. I asked my parents what I would have to do to have a computer like that for Christmas. I was already a good student, obedient, well-behaved. Surely I could earn it. My parents would just say computers were useless and I didn't really need one. What would I do with it? Play video games and become stupido? It was easy for them to find excuses not to buy things when we couldn't afford them. And that was often. I still think of that gray computer. I could have achieved everything if I had only possessed it.

A scratching in the wall. A sea of rodents. Rodents walking on rodents, hissing at other rodents.

And another terrible story: "Do you remember that girl? Tall, dark hair, blue eyes, kind of pretty. They lived down the street in Via San Cesareo, in that broken down house that used to be a horse stall. You played volleyball with her little brother in high school."

"Vaguely, Mamma. That was thirty years ago," I said. But I did remember her well, and she was indeed very pretty. She would walk through the street alone, wrapped in heavy clothes during winter, while I watched people from the window of my room.

"She killed herself. Last month. No one understood why."

Another anxious scratching inside the wall. The rodents frantically trying to escape. Rodents biting other rodents.

"We should sell," my wife said finally in the silence.

"And tell the buyers what? That the walls are haunted by rats?"

"Yes," she said.

Another Wednesday: "Guess what happened to Nicola?"

"Nicola? Who?"

"The peasant who lived near us. The one who went to jail for drugs, although I am sure he was set up. They all knew he was framed. He finally came out of jail. No one would speak to him. His wife had left. His children never visited. One day he was cutting an olive tree and fell from the tree. He hit his head on a rock. Dead immediately. There was nothing anyone could do."

Each story landed with the weight of casual fact. My mother presented each death as if it were weather, something that simply occurred, neither surprising nor preventable. And each time she told me of someone I had known, someone from a world I had left behind nearly 30 years before moving to Napoli for college and then to America. I would recall their faces, some small details, and now they were gone after living a life of many details I didn't know about. Falling in love, getting married, having children, pain, and disease.

It would begin small, almost apologetic, then grow. Louder. More insistent. More numerous, as if something were accumulating in the dark spaces behind the plaster, gathering, building its army.

I asked my wife if she noticed it. She looked at me strangely.

Even if my job didn't revolve around finding patterns, it was easy to notice the scratching always around the days I would have to wake up early to drive to college and talk to my mother.

"It's always after I talk to my mother," I said. "The scratching gets louder. For an hour or two afterward, it's worse."

What if the wall was not simply harboring rodents? Each death that entered my ear through the telephone entered the walls as well — names being recorded, catalogued, added to the wall's inventory of the gone.

The exterminator returned with boxes of poison. He set traps and sealed holes. For a few days the scratching continued, sometimes soft, sometimes violent, sometimes directly beneath my palm when I pressed it against the plaster in the dark.

The exterminator would come again to check the traps. The wall would scratch softly, patiently, waiting for the Wednesday mornings and telephone calls, waiting for each new name to be added to its record.

I still speak to my mother every Wednesday. I still drive to work while she tells me who has died, who has fallen, who cheats on his wife, who has given up. And I still hear the wall scratching in response, recording, remembering, keeping count.

Sometimes I wonder if she can hear it too, on her end of the line. That distant sound in the background. The sound of the wall keeping score.

Sometimes I wonder if all walls do this. If every house in every town contains a wall like mine, patient, scratching down the names of everyone we have ever known who has stopped being alive. If that is the case, we should not be afraid.
